turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry I'm late. The bus sat on the bridge for ages, then the rain came, and I nearly turned for home.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're grand, the slot is still yours. Rough enough out there?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Rough. And I'm in foul form, so don't mind me.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. What brought you down today?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): It's the waterworks. I'm up three or four times every night, the stream is weak, and then it dribbles.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long has that been going on?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Umm. I couldn't put a date on it. Last winter, or the one before. It just crept up.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): By day, does it take a while to get going?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Ages. I stand there like an eejit. Weak stream, and a dribble at the end. Mortifying.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any blood in the urine at all?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): No. No blood. I'd have noticed.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever, or have you been shivery?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): No fever. I'm just tired from the getting up, that's the height of it.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Has your weight changed at all?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Ah I don't know. The trousers are a bit looser, maybe, or maybe I'm imagining it. I haven't been on the scales.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any cough, or tightness in the chest?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Chest is grand. I don't be coughing.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): What are you drinking in the evenings?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): Tea. Two mugs, sometimes 3, after the news. Don't start on me.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): Are the nights worse when you've had the extra tea?
[SEG0021] person_1 (PATIENT): Suppose they are. Yeah. It still happens on the quiet nights, mind.
[SEG0022] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any other conditions, or tablets you're taking?
[SEG0023] person_1 (PATIENT): Blood pressure. Amladipine, five milligrams, every morning, for years. I'm seventy one. That's the lot.

[SEG0024] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll leave the amlodipine as it is. Err, my leaning is a benign enlarged prostate squeezing the pipe, though an overactive bladder is still possible. Infection looks unlikely with no fever and no blood, but I won't rule it out, and I'm not calling this definite today. The late tea is stirring the bladder as well.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll arrange a PSA blood test and a urine test, dip and culture. Reception can book the bloods. Leave the sample today if you can manage it.
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): I can manage the sample. I just want this sorted. I'm sick of trailing to the jacks all night.

[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): There's a tablet called tamsulosin, four hundred micrograms, once at night. It relaxes the prostate and can help the stream and the dribble. I won't start it today. If the urine is clear and the PSA isn't concerning, we'll start it when you're back.
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): Will that make me dizzy? I don't need that on top of the blood pressure tablet.

[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): It can drop the pressure a bit when you stand, especially with the amlodipine, so if we start it, take it at bedtime and sit a moment before you get up. We'll only go there if the tests are satisfactory. Ease off the tea after six, and try a decaf for the late mug if you can bear it.
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): I'll try. I'm not promising I'll be pleasant about the tea.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Come back in two weeks and we'll go through the results and decide on the tamsulosin then. Reception will have the blood form on your way out.

spec.situation: Older man getting up three to four times at night, weak stream, dribbling; drinks tea in the evening; denies blood in urine; PSA and urine tests planned, tamsulosin discussed.

traps.happens: The conversation OPENS with a remark, joke, apology for being late, small talk, or a trigger event (a relative's diagnosis, a neighbour's advice, the receptionist's note) BEFORE the real reason is stated. The patient states the real concern a few turns later.
traps.label_rule: chief_complaint is the real concern in a short phrase in the patient's wording (e.g. 'worried about diabetes', 'voice gets tired'). NOT the opening remark, the joke or the trigger (the relative's illness goes into family_history only if it is a relative's condition said as such).

traps.happens: The doctor asks only two to four review-of-systems questions (for example fever, weight, cough). Several other body systems are never asked about. One of the asked questions gets a vague or mixed answer.
traps.label_rule: negative_findings / review_of_systems ONLY for items the doctor actually asked AND the patient answered, evidence = that question and answer. Never add review-of-systems entries for systems nobody asked about, and never cite an unrelated turn (for example a turn about tiredness) for a system review.

features: vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.

doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.
